Unlike standard photometric optimization which minimizes pixel-wise reconstruction errors, these methods enforce that rendered image patches follow the distribution of real image patches, thereby suppressing artifacts and improving high-frequency details [S1, S2].

The claim states that the methods enforce rendered image patches to follow the distribution of real image patches to suppress artifacts and improve details, contrasting this with standard pixel-wise optimization. Source [S1] explicitly describes a 'local texture guidance' implemented via a 'patch discriminator' where 'patches randomly cropped from the reference view are regarded as real samples' and NeRF outputs are 'fake samples'. This adversarial setup forces the generated patches to match the distribution of real patches. The notes for [S1] confirm this addresses '2D image fidelity' and 'view-inconsistent rendered color and texture' (artifacts). Source [S2] supports the contrast by noting that removing adversarial objectives leads to 'blurry and uncanny' results, implying that the adversarial component is necessary for high-quality, high-frequency detail preservation. Thus, the evidence supports the claim.
